slides.title: Getting Started with Command Line

slides.title: Creating & Renaming
slides.body:
Creating & Renaming
Working with File System
Working with Files
Working with Directories
File/Folder Paths, Creating & Renaming
slides.notes: Alright, moving ahead, let’s take a look at the agenda for today’s session.  We’ll cover creating and renaming, working with files, directories, and understanding file and folder paths. By the end, you’ll know how to manage files easily from the command line."

slides.title: Working with Files
slides.body:
Files and File Systems
A file is a collection of related information that is stored
Files may have an extension which are used denote type of the file
Programs open and operate files based on the file extension
video.mp4
Image & Video: 
.jpeg, .png, .tiff, .mp4, .mov
index.html
Docs:
.html, .js, .py, .docx, .txt
slides.notes:
Let’s begin with the basics — files and file systems.A file is simply a collection of related information that’s stored on your computer.Each file usually has an extension, which tells us what type of file it is and how programs should handle it.
For example, an index.html file is an HTML document, while video.mp4 is a video file.Extensions like .jpeg, .png, and .tiff represent image files, .mp4 and .mov represent video files, and .html, .js, .py, .docx, or .txt represent documents or code.
So, the file extension plays an important role in helping both users and programs identify the nature of the file.
NXT

slides.title: Working with Files
slides.body:
Files and Folders
/home/teja/Pictures/Hello.png
C:\Users\teja\Pictures\Hello.png
Usually, we organize files in folders and these folders are stored in other folders and this continues until we arrive at
 C:\  drive or some other drive in Windows
Root directory ( / )in Linux-based systems and MacOS
slides.notes:
Now, files are not just stored randomly — we usually keep them organized inside folders. These folders can themselves contain more folders, and this nesting continues until we reach the root of the file system.
On Windows, the root is typically a drive like C:\. For example, the path C:\Users\teja\Pictures\Hello.png shows a file stored inside multiple folders under the C drive.
In Linux and MacOS, the root is represented by /. So, the same file path there would look like /home/teja/Pictures/Hello.png.
This way, the folder structure helps us locate and manage files in an organized manner.

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Creating a File
 touch  creates an empty file
$ touch practice.txt
$ ls
image.png             video.mp4           output.json
message.txt            Music                practice.txt
Bash
$ touch filename
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  touch.
slides.notes:
To create a new empty file, we use the touch command. The syntax is simple: touch filename.
For example, touch practice.txt will create a new file named practice.txt.
When we run ls afterward, we can see that the new file is added to the list of existing files and folders.

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Viewing File Content
 cat  reads contents of file and prints it
$ cat practice.txt
$ 
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  touch   cat.  
$ cat filename
Syntax
slides.notes:
To view the contents of a file, we use the cat command. The syntax is cat filename.
For example, if we run cat practice.txt, it will display whatever content is inside the file.

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Echo
 echo  output/prints a string in the terminal
$ echo "Hello world!"
Hello World!
Bash
Syntax
$ echo "content"
Commands we have learned so far:  touch   cat.  echo.
slides.notes:
echo is used to print text or output to the terminal. The syntax is echo "content".
For example, echo "Hello world!" will simply display Hello World! on the screen.

So now, along with touch,cat  we’ve also learned echo.

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Writing to Files Using echo Command
Using  >  operator we can redirect the output of echo command to a file
$ echo "Hello world!" > practice.txt
$ cat practice.txt
Hello World!
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  touch   cat.  echo.  
Syntax
$ echo "content" > filename
slides.notes:
echo can also be used to write content into a file using the > operator. The syntax is echo "content" > filename.
For example, echo "Hello world!" > practice.txt will create the file practice.txt with that content. When we check it with cat practice.txt, it shows Hello World!
So now, we’ve learned how to create files, view them, and also write into them.

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Renaming a File
$ mv practice.txt exam.txt
$ cat exam.txt
Hello World!
$ cat practice.txt
cat: practice.txt: No such file or directory
Bash
 mv  renames the file names
destination can be a new or existing file
Commands we have learned so far:  touch   cat   echo   mv.  
Syntax
$ mv source destination
slides.notes:
We’re looking at how to rename files using the mv command. It’s simple: you type mv, then the original file name, and then the new name. Like, mv practice.txt  exam.txt changes practice.txt to exam.txt. If you check with cat exam.txt, you’ll see the file’s content, but cat practice.txt gives an error since it’s gone. Cool, right? Why might you want to rename a file in a project?
Going forward, we’ve covered touch, cat, echo, and now mv. Next, we’ll explore more commands!

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Copying Files
 cp  copies src_file to dest_file
If dest_file already exist then cp overrides the contents of dest_file
$ cat exam.txt
Hello World!
$ cp exam.txt fun_text.txt
$ cat fun_text.txt
Hello World!
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  touch   cat   echo   mv   cp.  
Syntax
$ cp src_file dest_file
slides.notes:
Moving ahead, let’s talk about copying files. The command for this is cp, short for copy.
Here’s the idea: when you run cp exam.txt fun_text.txt, it creates a duplicate of exam.txt with the name fun_text.txt. Both files will now have the same content.
But here’s something important — if the destination file already exists, cp will overwrite it without warning.

So here’s a question for you: can you think of a scenario where overwriting an existing file accidentally could cause problems?

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Deleting a File
$ ls
image.png             video.mp4           fun_text.txt
message.txt            Music                exam.txt
$ rm exam.txt
$ ls
image.png             video.mp4          fun_text.txt
message.txt            Music                      
Bash
 rm   removes (delete) files
Commands we have learned so far:  touch   cat   echo   mv   cp   rm.   
Syntax
$ rm filename
slides.notes:
Alright, let's learn the "rm" command for deleting files.
The syntax is simple: rm filename
In our example, we first check our files with "ls", then remove exam.txt with "rm exam.txt". When we check again, the file is gone.
Remember: The rm command permanently deletes files with no recycling bin.
So far we've learned six key commands: touch, cat, echo, mv, cp, and rm.

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Hidden Files
Linux, by default, hides many of the sensitive system files, in order to avoid accidental changes
Hidden files starts with "."
slides.notes:
Next up, let's talk about hidden files in Linux.
Linux hides many sensitive system files by default. This is a safety feature to prevent accidental changes that might damage your system.
How can you identify hidden files? Simple - they always start with a dot "." character.
Let's move on to see how we can work with these hidden files.

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body:
Hidden Files
$ ls 
image.png             video.mp4           fun_text.txt
message.txt            Music                exam.txt
$ ls -a
.				   ..		             image.png        video.mp4           message.txt            Music               exam.txt	     fun_text.txt
.bashrc               .profile 
Bash
$ ls -a
Syntax
 ls -a   shows the hidden files
Commands we have learned so far:  touch   cat   echo   mv   cp   rm   ls -a.
slides.notes:
Moving on, to view hidden files we use "ls -a" command where "-a" means "all".
In our example, regular "ls" shows normal files, but "ls -a" reveals hidden files starting with dots like .bashrc and .profile. It also shows "." (current directory) and ".." (parent directory).
These hidden files typically contain important configurations, so handle with care.

slides.title: Working With Files
slides.body: Summary
slides.notes:
Let's take a moment to summarize what we've learned about working with files.
We've covered seven essential commands:
First, "touch" creates empty files. "Cat" displays file contents on screen. "Echo" writes text to standard output. "Mv" renames or moves files. "Cp" copies files or their contents. "Rm" permanently deletes files. And finally, "ls -a" reveals hidden files.
These commands form the foundation of file management in Linux. Which of these commands do you think you'll use most often?
tables: Reads contents of file and prints it

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.notes: Now let's move forward to our next topic that is working with directories.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Creating A Directory
 mkdir  creates a directory
$ mkdir tutorial
$ ls
image.png             video.mp4           exam.txt
message.txt            Music                tutorial
$ mkdir directory_name
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir
slides.notes:
To create a new directory, we use the "mkdir" command, which stands for "make directory." The syntax is simple: mkdir followed by the name you want to give your directory.
In our example, we use "mkdir tutorial" to create a directory named "tutorial." When we run the "ls" command to list our files, we can see our new directory appears alongside our existing files.
Directories are essential for organizing your files in a structured way, just like folders on your computer.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
$ pwd
/home/ib-developer
Current Working Directory
$ pwd 
Syntax
 pwd  prints name of current working directory
Current Working Directory Path
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd
slides.notes:
Next, let's see how to check our location in the file system.
The "pwd" command stands for "present working directory" and shows your current location.
In our example, typing "pwd" shows we're in "/home/ib-developer" - this is our current path.
This command is essential for knowing where you are before running other commands.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Changing the Current Working Directory
$ pwd
/home/ib-developer 
$ cd ./tutorial
$ pwd
/home/ib-developer/tutorial
Bash
 cd  changes the current working directory
$ cd directory_path
Syntax
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.
slides.notes:
Now let's learn how to move between directories.
The "cd" command stands for "change directory" and lets you navigate to different locations.
In our example, we first check our location with "pwd", showing we're in "/home/ib-developer".
Then we use "cd ./tutorial" to move into the tutorial directory. The "./" means "in the current directory".
When we check again with "pwd", we see we're now in "/home/ib-developer/tutorial".
We've now learned three key directory commands: mkdir, pwd, and cd.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Creating a Directory in Directory
 mkdir  creates a directory
$ mkdir directory_name
Syntax
$ mkdir notes
$ ls
notes
$ cd notes
$ pwd
/home/ib-developer/tutorial/notes
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.
Bash
slides.notes:
Next, let's create directories inside other directories.
Using "mkdir notes", we create a subdirectory. We confirm it exists with "ls".
We then navigate into it with "cd notes" and confirm our new location with "pwd".
This is how we build nested directory structures for better organization.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Switching to Parent Directory
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/home/ib-developer/tutorial
Bash
 cd ..  move to parent directory
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd...  
.. is relative path to parent directory
slides.notes:
Now let's learn how to move back up a directory.
The shorthand ".." represents the parent directory, and "cd .." takes you one level up.
In our example, after using "cd ..", "pwd" shows we've moved from the notes folder back up to "/home/ib-developer/tutorial".
This navigation technique is essential for moving efficiently between directories.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
File Paths
There are two notations for file paths
Absolute Path: Representing the complete path of a file or folder from the root
Relative Path: Representing the path of a file or folder wrt. current working directory
slides.notes:
Now, let's talk about two important path types:
Absolute paths start from the root directory and show the complete location.
Relative paths show location based on your current directory.
Both are essential for effective navigation. Think of absolute as a full address and relative as directions from your current spot.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
File Paths
DNo: 10-13/2,
MVP Colony,
Vivekananda Street,
Gachibowli,
Hyderabad
From here go straight for 30m 
and your destination is 
4th house on your right
Absolute Path
Relative Path
slides.notes:
Here's a simple analogy for file paths:
An absolute path is like a complete address - "DNo: 10-13/2, MVP Colony, Vivekananda Street, Gachibowli, Hyderabad." It works from anywhere because it contains all location details.
A relative path is like directions from your current spot - "Go straight for 30m and your destination is 4th house on your right." It only works if you know your starting point.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Absolute and Relative File Paths
In relative path conventions:
.  refers to the current working directory.  
..  refers to the parent directory.
/home/parent/child
.
..
CWD:   /home/parent/child
../..
slides.notes:
Let's look at path conventions with a practical example.
Our current working directory (CWD) is "/home/parent/child".
In relative paths:
The single dot "." represents your current directory (/home/parent/child)
Double dots ".." represent the parent directory (/home/parent)
If we use "../.." we'd go up two levels to "/home".
These shortcuts help us navigate efficiently without typing full paths.
Remember these symbols as they're used frequently in Linux navigation.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
File Paths
Current Working Directory:   /home/ib-developer
Absolute Path
/home/ib-developer/tutorial
Relative Path
/flower.png
/home/hello.png
../../flower.png
../hello.png
./tutorial
slides.notes:
Here are examples comparing relative and absolute paths from "/home/ib-developer":
"./tutorial" is equivalent to "/home/ib-developer/tutorial" "../hello.png" is equivalent to "/home/hello.png" "../../flower.png" is equivalent to "/flower.png"
Relative paths navigate based on your current location using dots, while absolute paths give complete locations from root.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Using Absolute Path
$ pwd
/home/ib-developer/tutorial
$ cd /home/ib-developer
$ pwd
/home/ib-developer
Bash
Change working directory using absolute path
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd...
slides.notes:
Now let's see how to use absolute paths with the cd command.
In our example, we start in "/home/ib-developer/tutorial" as shown by pwd.
Then we use "cd /home/ib-developer" - this absolute path takes us directly to that location regardless of where we started from.
When we check with pwd again, we confirm we've moved to "/home/ib-developer".
Absolute paths are useful when you need to jump to a specific location from anywhere in the system.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Home Directory
 cd ~.   command can be used to switch to home directory
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd...  cd ~.   
$ cd ~
$ pwd
/home/ib-developer
Bash
slides.notes:
Here's another quick way to get home.
Simply typing "cd" with a space and no target will also take you to your home directory.
This works exactly like "cd ~" that we just saw, bringing you to "/home/ib-developer" in our example.
This is probably the fastest shortcut to return home when navigating.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Changing the Current Working Directory
 cd /  changes your current directory to root folder
$ cd /
$ pwd
/
Bash
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd...  cd ~.  cd /.
slides.notes:
Now let's learn how to navigate to the root directory.
The command "cd /" takes you to the root directory, which is the top-level directory in your system.
In our example, after using "cd /", we confirm with pwd that we're now at "/" - the root of the entire file system.
The root directory contains all other directories and files in your system.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Renaming a Directory
$ cd ..
$ ls
message.txt   python_files   tutorial  welcome.txt  notes
$ mv tutorial commands
$ ls
message.txt        python_files      commands   welcome.txt
 mv  renames the directory name
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd... cd ~   cd /. .mv.   
Bash
$ mv source destination
Syntax
slides.notes:
For renaming directories, we use the same "mv" command we learned for files.
In our example, "mv tutorial commands" renames the tutorial directory to commands.
We confirm the change with "ls" and see tutorial is now called commands.
The "mv" command works identically for both files and directories.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Moving a Directory
$ cd ..
$ ls
message.txt   python_files   tutorial  welcome.txt  notes
$ mv welcome.txt commands
$ cd commands
$ ls commands
welcome.txt
 mv  moves files or directories from source to destination  paths
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd... cd ~   cd /. .mv.   
Bash
$ mv source destination
Syntax
slides.notes:
Now let's see how to move files between directories.
The "mv" command also moves files or directories from one location to another.
In our example, we first go up a directory and list contents.
Then we move "welcome.txt" into the "commands" directory using "mv welcome.txt commands".
When we navigate into the commands directory and check, we see welcome.txt is now there.
This is how you can organize your files by moving them between directories.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Copying Files to Another Directory
 cp  can be used to copy files between directories
$ cd commands
$ ls
countries.txt
$ cd ..
$ cp welcome.txt commands
$ cd commands
$ ls
countries.txt      welcome.txt
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd.... cd ~.  cd /. .mv. .cp. 
Bash
$ cp file_path directory_name
Syntax
slides.notes:
The "cp" command lets us copy files between directories.
The syntax is "cp file_path directory_name" to copy a file to another location.
In our example, we first check what's in the commands directory - just countries.txt.
Then we navigate up, copy welcome.txt to commands with "cp welcome.txt commands".
When we go back to commands and check, we now have both countries.txt and welcome.txt.
Unlike "mv" which moves files, "cp" keeps the original and creates a copy at the destination.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Copying Directory
 cp -r  can be used to copy a directory
$ cd ..
$ mkdir linux
$ cp -r commands linux
$ cd linux
$ ls
countries.txt      welcome.txt
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd ..  cd ~.  cd /. .mv.  .cp. .cp -r. 
Bash
$ cp -r source_path destination_path
Syntax
slides.notes:
For copying entire directories, we need to add the "-r" flag to the cp command.
The "r" stands for recursive, meaning it copies the directory and everything inside it.
In our example, we go up a directory, create a new "linux" directory, then copy our entire "commands" directory into it with "cp -r commands linux".
When we check inside linux, we see all the files from commands were copied over.
This is useful for backing up folders or creating directory structures.
Remember: Without the -r flag, cp won't work on directories.

slides.title: Copying Directory
slides.body:
Common Mistake
Raises an error if destination path have any non existing directories in between
$ cp -r home/ib-developer/commands/notes  home/ib-developer/some-random/new-dir
cp: cannot create directory 'home/ib-developer/some-random/new-dir': No such file or directory
Commands we have learned so far:  mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd ..  cd ~.  cd /. .mv.  .cp. .cp -r. 
Bash
slides.notes:
Here's a common error when copying directories.
When copying to a path with non-existent intermediate directories, cp -r fails.
In our example, the copy fails because "some-random" directory doesn't exist.
The error message clearly shows the problem.
Remember to create any missing directories before copying.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body:
Deleting a Directory
$ ls
message.txt                  python_files   	commands   welcome.txt
$ rm -r commands
$ ls
message.txt                python_files    welcome.txt  
$ rm -r directory_name
Syntax
 rm -r   removes(deletes) directories 
Commands we have learned so far:   mkdir   pwd   cd.  cd ...  cd ~.  cd /. .mv. .cp. .cp -r.  .rm -r.
Bash
slides.notes:
To delete directories, we use "rm -r" where the "-r" flag means recursive deletion.
In our example, we first list our files with "ls" and see the commands directory.
Then we delete it with "rm -r commands" and verify with "ls" that it's gone.
Be very careful with this command - it permanently deletes everything in the directory!
We've now learned "rm -r" for removing directories.

slides.title: Working with Directories
slides.body: Summary
slides.notes:
Let's summarize what we've learned about directory commands:
First, "mkdir" creates new directories.
"Pwd" shows your current location in the file system.
"Cd" followed by a path changes your directory.
"Cd .." moves up to the parent directory.
"Cd ~" takes you to your home directory.
And "cd /" navigates to the root directory.
These six commands are essential for navigating the Linux file system effectively.Along with this we have also learned mv, cp , cp -r , rm -r.
tables: Prints name of current working directory
Used to switch to home directory
changes your current directory to root folder

These directory skills help you maintain an organized file system.
